A 4-month-old boy’s mother notices that his left foot curves inwards. The lateral border of the foot is convex (bean-shaped), the heel is in neutral with normal ankle dorsiflexion, and the forefoot can be passively abducted past neutral. A heel bisector line passes through the 4th toe.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcq.e: Forefoot adduction at the tarsometatarsal joints with a normal hindfoot is metatarsus adductus, the typical cause of intoeing in infants. The heel bisector passing lateral to the second toe confirms forefoot adduction. Clubfoot has heel equinus and varus. Tibial torsion and femoral anteversion present in toddlers and older children. Most flexible cases resolve by 4-6 months or with stretching.
w: Correct - forefoot adduction with a normal heel = metatarsus adductus.
Wrong - clubfoot has a rigid equinus and varus heel.
Wrong - tibial torsion presents in toddlers with a negative thigh-foot angle.
Wrong - femoral anteversion presents at 3-8 years with increased hip internal rotation.
Wrong - vertical talus is a rigid rocker-bottom foot.

mcq.stem:
A 2-year-old girl trips frequently and her feet point inwards when she walks. Lying prone with knees flexed, her thigh-foot angle is -20°. Hip internal and external rotation are symmetrical and normal, and her patellae face forwards when standing.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Denis Browne bar at night for one year
Twister cables worn during the day
mcq.e: A negative thigh-foot angle with normal hip rotation and forward-facing patellae means internal tibial torsion, the typical cause of intoeing in toddlers. It resolves spontaneously, usually before school age, and braces or twister cables do not change its natural history. A supramalleolar osteotomy is considered only if it persists beyond about 8 years with functional problems.
w: Wrong - night splints have no proven benefit.
Wrong - osteotomy is only for persistence beyond ~8 years.
Wrong - twister cables are ineffective and outdated.
Wrong - the femur is normal here (hip rotation symmetrical).
Correct - internal tibial torsion resolves spontaneously in most children.

mcq.stem:
A 6-year-old girl intoes and ‘trips over her own feet’. She prefers to sit with her knees together and her feet out to the sides of her bottom. Standing, her patellae point towards each other. Prone, hip internal rotation is 80° and external rotation 20°; the thigh-foot angle is +10°.
What is the most likely cause of her intoeing?
mcq.e: W-sitting, ‘kissing’ patellae and increased hip internal rotation with reduced external rotation are the signs of increased femoral anteversion, the usual cause of intoeing at 3-8 years. A normal thigh-foot angle excludes tibial torsion. Most cases resolve; derotational osteotomy is considered only if it persists past 9-10 years with functional problems.
w: Wrong - tibial torsion gives a negative thigh-foot angle with forward patellae.
Wrong - metatarsus adductus is a forefoot deformity of infancy.
Correct - excessive hip IR + W-sitting + inward patellae = femoral anteversion.
Wrong - nothing suggests a previous clubfoot (equinus, varus, scars).
Wrong - no spasticity or developmental delay is described.

mcq.stem:
A 6-year-old boy has had an intermittent limp for 3 months, with occasional aching in the right thigh after football. He is afebrile and well. Right hip abduction and internal rotation are reduced. ESR and CRP are normal. The AP pelvis shows a smaller, sclerotic right femoral epiphysis with widening of the medial joint space.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcq.e: A boy aged 4-10 with an insidious, mostly painless limp, loss of abduction and internal rotation and normal inflammatory markers fits Perthes disease. The small dense epiphysis with medial joint space widening is the initial (necrotic) stage. Transient synovitis is acute with a normal X-ray, septic arthritis is febrile with raised markers, and SCFE affects obese adolescents.
w: Wrong - transient synovitis is acute, short-lived and the X-ray is normal.
Wrong - septic arthritis is acute and febrile with raised inflammatory markers.
Wrong - SCFE affects adolescents and shows physeal widening or a slip.
Wrong - JIA causes synovitis with raised markers and no epiphyseal sclerosis.
Correct - typical age, chronic limp, loss of abduction/IR and epiphyseal sclerosis.

mcq.stem:
A 5-year-old girl woke up limping 2 days after a viral upper respiratory infection. Temperature 37.4 °C. She can bear weight with a limp, and hip internal rotation is mildly painful. WBC 8.5 ×10⁹/L, ESR 12 mm/h, CRP 4 mg/L. Ultrasound shows a small hip effusion; the X-ray is normal.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcq.e: Lecturer pearl: Kocher criteria for septic hip are fever over 38.5 °C, non-weight bearing, ESR over 40 and WBC over 12. With 0 of 4 positive after a viral illness, this is transient synovitis – self-limiting, treated with rest, NSAIDs and review. Perthes is chronic and shows epiphyseal changes on X-ray, and SCFE affects adolescents.
w: Wrong - septic arthritis is febrile, non-weight bearing with raised markers.
Wrong - Perthes is insidious with radiographic epiphyseal changes.
Correct - post-viral, afebrile, weight bearing, normal markers = transient synovitis.
Wrong - SCFE affects adolescents, usually obese.
Wrong - osteomyelitis gives fever, raised markers and bony tenderness.

mcq.stem:
A 3-year-old boy has refused to walk for 24 hours. Temperature 39.2 °C. He lies with the left hip flexed, abducted and externally rotated and screams on any movement. WBC 18 ×10⁹/L, ESR 60 mm/h, CRP 110 mg/L. Ultrasound shows a large hip effusion.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Oral NSAIDs and review in 48 hours
MRI of the pelvis under sedation
mcq.e: Lecturer pearl: all four Kocher criteria are positive, so septic arthritis is very likely. This is a surgical emergency: aspirate (send for culture), then arthrotomy and washout with IV antibiotics. Pus under pressure in the hip can destroy the cartilage and cause AVN within hours. Containment bracing is a Perthes treatment.
w: Wrong - NSAIDs and waiting treat transient synovitis, not a septic joint.
Correct - septic hip needs emergency drainage and IV antibiotics.
Wrong - MRI delays drainage when the diagnosis is already clear.
Wrong - traction does not drain the infection.
Wrong - containment is for Perthes disease, not infection.

mcq.stem:
A 6-year-old boy with Perthes disease is now in the fragmentation stage. He has a mild limp and 30° of hip abduction. His parents ask about his long-term outlook.
Which finding is associated with the poorest prognosis?
o: Symptom onset at 5 years of age
Lateral pillar intact at full height
Widening of the medial joint space
mcq.e: In the fragmentation stage the Herring lateral pillar classification predicts outcome. Group C (less than 50% of pillar height kept) has a poor prognosis, and group A (intact) a very good one. Younger age at onset (under 6-8 years) is favourable because there is more time to remodel. Medial joint widening and a cold bone scan are diagnostic features present in most cases, not prognostic markers.
w: Wrong - young onset is a good prognostic factor.
Wrong - an intact pillar (Herring A) has a very good prognosis.
Wrong - this is an early diagnostic sign, not a prognostic one.
Correct - Herring C (< 50% pillar height) = poor prognosis.
Wrong - reduced uptake is expected in Perthes and does not grade prognosis.

mcq.stem:
A 9-year-old boy developed Perthes disease 4 months ago. He has persistent loss of abduction despite physiotherapy. X-ray in the fragmentation stage shows the lateral pillar at about 50% height with early lateral extrusion, and an arthrogram shows that the head can be contained in abduction.
What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: In situ screw fixation of the epiphysis
mcq.e: Age over 8 at onset, Herring B/C, lateral extrusion and persistent loss of motion are indications for surgical containment. When the head can be contained, a proximal femoral varus osteotomy (or pelvic osteotomy) redirects it deep into the acetabulum so it remodels round. A valgus osteotomy is a salvage procedure for hinge abduction, which is not present here.
w: Correct - containable head + poor prognostic factors = varus osteotomy.
Wrong - observation is for young children with good prognostic features.
Wrong - in situ fixation treats SCFE, not Perthes.
Wrong - valgus osteotomy is only for non-containable hinge abduction.
Wrong - arthroplasty is not an option in a 9-year-old with a remodelling head.

mcq.stem:
An 8-year-old girl with Perthes disease is being planned for possible containment surgery. The surgeon needs to see, dynamically, whether the cartilaginous femoral head can be seated within the acetabulum in abduction or whether it hinges on the lateral lip.
Which investigation provides this information?
mcq.e: An arthrogram outlines the cartilaginous head and shows dynamically whether it is covered and contained in abduction, or whether it hinges on the lateral acetabular lip (hinge abduction). This decides between a varus containment osteotomy and a salvage valgus osteotomy. MRI shows the extent of necrosis, a bone scan shows a cold area, and plain films show only the ossified part.
w: Wrong - MRI shows necrosis extent but is static.
Wrong - a bone scan shows perfusion, not containment.
Correct - arthrography shows containment and hinge abduction dynamically.
Wrong - CT shows bone, not the cartilage head, and is static.
Wrong - plain films show only the ossified epiphysis.

mcq.stem:
A 13-year-old boy with a BMI of 31 has had aching in his left knee for 5 weeks and now walks with a limp. Examination of the knee is normal. When the left hip is passively flexed it rolls into external rotation, and internal rotation is reduced.
What is the most appropriate investigation?
o: AP pelvis and frog-leg lateral X-rays
AP and lateral radiographs of the left knee
MRI of the left knee to assess the menisci
mcq.e: Knee pain in an obese adolescent with obligatory external rotation on hip flexion (Drehmann sign) is SCFE until proven otherwise – hip pain is referred to the knee via the obturator nerve. The investigation is an AP pelvis and frog-leg lateral (cross-table lateral if the slip may be unstable). Knee imaging would be normal and delay diagnosis.
w: Correct - AP pelvis + frog-leg lateral shows the slip.
Wrong - the knee is normal; this is the classic knee pain trap.
Wrong - knee MRI misses the hip pathology.
Wrong - ultrasound shows an effusion but not the slip.
Wrong - he is afebrile with a mechanical picture; bloods do not make the diagnosis.

mcq.stem:
A 12-year-old boy with obesity falls from a bicycle and cannot stand even with crutches. The hip X-ray shows a moderate slip of the right capital femoral epiphysis. He is admitted for surgery.
Which of the following should be AVOIDED?
o: Forceful closed reduction of the slip
Assessing the opposite hip on X-ray
mcq.e: This is an unstable slip (Loder: cannot weight bear even with crutches), which already carries a high AVN risk. Forceful manipulation stretches or tears the retinacular vessels and raises that risk further, so it must be avoided. Standard care is non-weight bearing, urgent in situ fixation with a single cannulated screw, counselling about AVN, and assessment of the other hip.
w: Wrong - non-weight bearing is appropriate to prevent further slip.
Wrong - in situ screw fixation is the standard treatment.
Wrong - AVN counselling is essential in an unstable slip.
Correct - forceful reduction risks AVN and must be avoided.
Wrong - the contralateral hip should always be assessed (bilateral in ~25%).

mcq.stem:
A 14-year-old girl presents with left groin pain and a limp after a minor stumble. X-rays confirm a slipped capital femoral epiphysis, and the registrar is counselling the family about the risk of avascular necrosis.
Which feature best predicts a high AVN risk?
o: Symptoms present for longer than three weeks
Obesity with a body mass index over 30
Knee pain as the presenting complaint
mcq.e: Lecturer pearl: the Loder classification is based on stability. A slip is unstable if the child cannot weight bear even with crutches; the AVN risk is then up to about 50%, compared with under 10% for stable slips. Symptom duration (acute vs chronic) and obesity are less useful in predicting AVN.
w: Wrong - a chronic course suggests a stable slip with a lower AVN risk.
Correct - an unstable (Loder) slip carries the highest AVN risk.
Wrong - obesity is a risk factor for SCFE, not a predictor of AVN.
Wrong - bilaterality affects follow-up, not AVN risk in the slipped hip.
Wrong - referred knee pain causes delay but does not grade AVN risk.

mcq.stem:
A 9-year-old girl below the 10th centile for height and on the 50th for weight presents with a painful limp. She has been tired, constipated and gaining weight, and her teacher notes that she is always cold. X-ray shows a left slipped capital femoral epiphysis.
Which additional investigation is most important?
o: Bone age X-ray of the hand
mcq.e: SCFE in a child under 10, or in one who is short or not obese, is atypical and needs an endocrine work-up: TSH, free T4 and serum creatinine. Fatigue, constipation, weight gain and cold intolerance point to hypothyroidism. An endocrine cause is also an indication for prophylactic fixation of the other hip because the risk of a bilateral slip is high.
w: Wrong - GH deficiency is a cause, but her symptoms point to the thyroid.
Wrong - vitamin D deficiency does not explain cold intolerance and constipation.
Wrong - HLA-B27 is for spondyloarthropathy, not SCFE.
Wrong - bone age may be delayed but does not identify the cause.
Correct - hypothyroid features in an atypical SCFE = check thyroid function.

mcq.stem:
An 11-year-old boy with end-stage renal disease on haemodialysis (renal osteodystrophy) presents with a stable right slipped capital femoral epiphysis. His left hip is asymptomatic and its X-ray is normal.
In addition to in situ fixation of the right hip, what is the most appropriate management of the left hip?
o: Clinical review only if pain develops
mcq.e: Lecturer pearl: prophylactic pinning of the contralateral hip is advised when SCFE has an endocrine or metabolic cause (renal osteodystrophy, hypothyroidism, GH therapy), in young children with a lot of growth remaining, and when follow-up is unreliable. Renal osteodystrophy carries a very high risk of a bilateral slip. Otherwise the opposite hip is observed.
w: Correct - metabolic SCFE = prophylactic contralateral fixation.
Wrong - waiting for pain risks an unstable contralateral slip.
Wrong - observation is for typical slips, not metabolic ones.
Wrong - bracing does not prevent a slip.
Wrong - there is no slip to reduce on the left.

mcq.stem:
A 12-year-old boy has a painful limp. On the AP pelvic X-ray, a line drawn along the superior border of the left femoral neck does not intersect any part of the left capital femoral epiphysis, whereas on the right it crosses the lateral epiphysis.
What is this radiological sign called?
mcq.e: The line along the superior femoral neck is Klein’s line; when it fails to intersect the epiphysis, Trethowan’s sign is positive and indicates SCFE. Drehmann sign is a clinical sign (external rotation on flexion). The crescent sign is a subchondral fracture in Perthes. The Steel blanch sign is a metaphyseal double density on the AP view (Lecturer pearl). Note: the slide lists Trethowan’s sign alongside MRI findings; it is a plain X-ray sign.
w: Wrong - Drehmann sign is a clinical examination finding.
Wrong - the crescent sign is a subchondral fracture in Perthes/AVN.
Wrong - Steel blanch is a metaphyseal double-density sign, not Klein’s line.
Wrong - Shenton’s line is used in DDH.
Correct - Klein’s line missing the epiphysis = Trethowan sign.

mcq.stem:
A 2-day-old first-born girl delivered by caesarean section for breech presentation is examined. At rest the hip is located. With the hip flexed and adducted, gentle posterior pressure makes the femoral head slip out of the acetabulum with a palpable clunk, and it returns when the hip is abducted.
How is this hip best classified?
mcq.e: Classification is based on the resting position. This hip is located at rest and dislocates with the Barlow manoeuvre, so it is ‘reduced but dislocatable’ (Barlow positive). An Ortolani-positive hip is dislocated at rest and reduces on abduction. The reduction seen here only follows the dislocation the examiner provoked. It needs ultrasound and Pavlik harness treatment.
w: Wrong - a stable dysplastic hip does not dislocate on Barlow.
Wrong - this hip is located at rest, not dislocated.
Correct - located at rest, dislocates on Barlow = reduced but dislocatable.
Wrong - this hip reduces easily, so it is not irreducible.
Wrong - a hip that dislocates with a clunk is pathological, not physiological laxity.

mcq.stem:
A 6-week-old first-born girl was delivered vaginally from a frank breech presentation. Her hip examination today, including the Barlow and Ortolani tests, is normal and abduction is symmetrical.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: MRI of both hips under sedation
Pelvic X-ray when she starts walking
mcq.e: She has three of the 4 F’s (female, first-born, frank breech), so a hip ultrasound is indicated even though the examination is normal; clinical tests miss dysplasia of a stable hip. Ultrasound is the imaging of choice before about 4-6 months, while the femoral head is cartilage (Graf alpha ≥ 60° is normal). Radiographs are used once the ossific nucleus appears.
w: Wrong - the femoral head is not yet ossified, so X-ray is unreliable.
Correct - risk factors justify ultrasound under 4-6 months.
Wrong - breech + female + first-born warrants screening ultrasound.
Wrong - MRI is not a screening tool for DDH.
Wrong - waiting until walking misses the window for Pavlik treatment.

mcq.stem:
A 4-month-old girl with a dislocated, Ortolani-positive left hip has worn a Pavlik harness full-time for 4 weeks. Ultrasound today shows that the femoral head remains dislocated.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Continue the harness for another 8 weeks
Tighten the straps to 120° of hip flexion
mcq.e: The Pavlik harness should be stopped if the hip has not reduced within 3-4 weeks. Continuing risks erosion of the posterior acetabular wall (Pavlik disease) without achieving reduction. The next step is closed reduction (with arthrogram ± adductor tenotomy) and hip spica. Excessive flexion causes femoral nerve palsy, and open reduction is for failed closed reduction or children over 18 months.
w: Wrong - persisting with a failed harness damages the posterior acetabulum.
Wrong - hyperflexion causes femoral nerve palsy and does not reduce the hip.
Wrong - open reduction comes after failed closed reduction or age > 18 months.
Correct - Pavlik failure at 3-4 weeks → closed reduction and spica.
Wrong - delaying leaves the hip dislocated during the key growth period.

mcq.stem:
A 6-week-old boy is being treated with a Pavlik harness for DDH; his parents have been adjusting the straps at home. At review his mother says he no longer kicks with his right leg. There is no active knee extension and no visible quadriceps contraction, while hip abduction looks normal.
Which harness error is most likely responsible?
mcq.e: Lecturer pearl: in a Pavlik harness, excessive hip flexion stretches the femoral nerve under the inguinal ligament and causes femoral nerve palsy (loss of quadriceps activity). Excessive or forced abduction causes avascular necrosis, and tight shoulder straps can cause brachial plexus palsy. Femoral nerve palsy is managed by removing the harness until quadriceps function recovers.
w: Wrong - excessive abduction causes AVN, not nerve palsy.
Wrong - tight shoulder straps cause brachial plexus palsy.
Wrong - insufficient flexion risks failure of reduction, not nerve palsy.
Correct - hyperflexion = femoral nerve palsy.
Wrong - loose posterior straps reduce abduction; they do not injure the femoral nerve.

mcq.stem:
A 2½-year-old girl walks with a lurching limp. Her left leg is 2 cm shorter and abduction is limited. The AP pelvis shows the left femoral head ossific nucleus lying above Hilgenreiner’s line and lateral to Perkin’s line, with a broken Shenton’s line.
What is the most appropriate management?
mcq.e: Treatment of DDH depends on age: Pavlik harness under 6 months, closed reduction and spica at 6-18 months, and open reduction (± femoral shortening or pelvic osteotomy) after 18 months. At 2½ years soft-tissue contractures and an adaptive acetabulum make closed reduction unlikely to succeed. The radiographic lines confirm a dislocated hip.
w: Wrong - the Pavlik harness is for infants under 6 months.
Correct - over 18 months = open reduction ± osteotomy.
Wrong - closed reduction is for 6-18 months and usually fails at this age.
Wrong - a brace cannot reduce an established dislocation.
Wrong - an untreated dislocation leads to limp, deformity and early arthritis.

mcq.stem:
An 18-month-old boy who walked at 11 months has bowed legs noticed by his grandmother. The bowing is symmetrical, with a gentle curve involving both femur and tibia, and there is no lateral thrust. His height is on the 50th centile and his wrists are normal. Standing X-ray: metaphyseal-diaphyseal angle 8° on both sides; physes normal.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcq.e: Under 2 years, symmetrical gentle bowing of both femur and tibia with a metaphyseal-diaphyseal angle under about 9-11° is physiological and resolves, often swinging into valgus at 3-4 years. Blount disease shows abrupt proximal tibial angulation, lateral thrust and an angle over 11° (Lecturer pearl). Rickets causes widened wrists, metaphyseal cupping and fraying and a raised ALP.
w: Wrong - Blount shows an abrupt proximal tibial angle > 11° and lateral thrust.
Wrong - rickets has widened wrists and metaphyseal cupping and fraying.
Wrong - achondroplasia causes short stature and rhizomelia.
Wrong - adolescent Blount occurs after 10 years.
Correct - young, symmetrical, gentle curve, normal angle = physiological.

mcq.stem:
A 2½-year-old obese girl who walked at 9 months has progressive bowing of both legs and a lateral thrust of the knees on walking. Standing X-ray shows medial metaphyseal beaking of both proximal tibiae and a metaphyseal-diaphyseal angle of 15°, consistent with Langenskiöld stage II. Her bone profile is normal.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Reassurance and review in a year
mcq.e: This is infantile Blount disease (early walker, obese, bilateral, medial beaking, angle over 11°). Under 3 years with Langenskiöld stage I-II, a knee-ankle-foot orthosis worn for about 2 years can allow the bony changes to resolve. Osteotomy is indicated for stage I-II over 3 years, stage III-VI, any stage over 4 years, brace failure, or an angle over 20°.
w: Correct - < 3 years and stage I-II = KAFO.
Wrong - progressive Blount should not just be observed.
Wrong - osteotomy is for older children, higher stages or brace failure.
Wrong - the bone profile is normal; this is not rickets.
Wrong - guided growth is mainly used in older children and adolescents.

mcq.stem:
A 13-year-old obese boy (BMI 34) has progressive bowing of the right leg over 2 years, with medial knee ache. The left leg is straight. X-ray shows varus arising from the proximal tibia with a widened medial physis; the distal femur is in mild varus.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Reassurance; it will resolve with growth
Weight loss alone with annual review
mcq.e: Adolescent Blount disease (over 10 years, usually unilateral, obese) is progressive and does not resolve spontaneously, and bracing is ineffective. Treatment is surgical: a proximal tibial valgus osteotomy, or guided growth while the physis is still open. Weight loss helps but does not correct an established deformity.
w: Wrong - bracing works only in infantile Blount under 3 years.
Wrong - adolescent Blount progresses and does not resolve.
Correct - adolescent Blount needs surgical correction.
Wrong - weight loss alone does not correct established varus.
Wrong - there is no metabolic bone disease to treat.
